title: Propene and HBr
subtitle: Markovnikov addition through the more stable cation

reactants.caption: propene + hydrogen bromide
reactants.learnerPrompt: The alkene reacts with HBr. Draw the first step.
hintTiers: The alkene π bond is the nucleophile. What is the electrophile in H–Br?
The π bond takes the proton, and the H–Br bond breaks onto bromine. Put the H on the end carbon so the cation is on the carbon with more alkyl groups. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: from the C=C π bond to the H, forming a bond from the CH₂ carbon to H. Arrow 2: from the H–Br bond onto bromine.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That puts the proton on the middle carbon and leaves a primary cation on the CH₂ end. Primary cations are very unstable. Put the H on the CH₂ carbon so the charge is on the secondary carbon.
The alkene is electron-rich, so it is the nucleophile here, not the target of one. Start from the π bond.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right start. Hydrogen can only have one bond: break the H–Br bond onto bromine.

cation.caption: isopropyl cation + bromide
hintTiers: Which species is the nucleophile now, and where is the positive charge?
Bromide gives a lone pair to the positively charged carbon. One arrow.
From a bromide lone pair to the central carbon, forming the C–Br bond.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That takes the proton back off and gives propene and HBr again: the reverse of the step you just drew. Bromide adds to the cation instead.

steps.explanationAfterStep: Protonation at the CH₂ end gives the secondary isopropyl cation, not the primary propyl cation. This is the slow step and it decides where the bromine ends up.
Bromide traps the cation: 2-bromopropane, the Markovnikov product. Hardly any 1-bromopropane forms.

mechanismSummary: The π bond takes the proton of HBr. The proton goes to the CH₂ end, so the positive charge sits on the secondary carbon, the more stable cation (Markovnikov's rule). Bromide then adds to that carbon: 2-bromopropane.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 20
